query: The (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy provides a large caloric response under applied-field and pressure-field operation but has poor integrity and tends to crack. Prior studies on related MM′X materials used epoxy-containing Mn0.98CoGe, obtaining compressive strengths of 152 and 218 MPa at two epoxy contents, and low-melting In composites, obtaining 48 MPa compressive strength and more than eight times the thermal conductivity of epoxy-containing samples under the reported conditions. These routes demonstrated gains in selected strength or heat-transport metrics, but the desired coexistence of robust integrity and high caloric performance remains unresolved. The target should also remain rare-earth-free. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing caloric response? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, quantitative or directional outcomes relative to the unchanged alloy, boundary conditions under applied-field, pressure, temperature, and loading regimes, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive controlled experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Microalloying the (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy with approximately 2 atomic percent Nb will lead to the in situ formation of a fine, ductile Nb‐rich precipitate network along grain boundaries, which will arrest crack propagation and improve compressive strength and fracture toughness while preserving the intrinsic caloric performance within ±5% of the unmodified alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy with excellent caloric response but poor mechanical integrity (prone to cracking).
generation.intervention: Addition of approximately 2 at% Nb (a rare-earth–free ductilizer) via microalloying.
generation.conditions: Identical applied-field and pressure-field regimes, operating in the temperature range where the caloric phase transformation occurs, and under similar compressive loading conditions as in previous studies.
generation.structural_mediator: A fine network of ductile Nb‐rich precipitates formed preferentially at grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: The Nb addition is expected to promote the nucleation of a coherent, ductile secondary phase at the grain boundaries. This secondary phase impedes crack propagation (thus enhancing mechanical integrity) while not significantly interfering with the phase transformation responsible for the caloric effect.
generation.predicted_outcome: The Nb-modified alloy should demonstrate a marked improvement in compressive strength (targeting values >200 MPa) and fracture toughness compared to the unmodified alloy, with the caloric response remaining within ±5% of that observed in the baseline material.
generation.baseline: The unmodified (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy, which shows excellent caloric performance but suffers from low mechanical integrity and crack propagation.
generation.boundary: Results are expected under the same operational fields (magnetic and pressure), temperature ranges of the caloric transition, and compressive test conditions previously reported. The intervention should not involve any extrinsic binder or low-melting phase addition.
generation.uncertainty: While analogous systems suggest that minor Nb additions can improve mechanical properties without compromising functional performance, the precise balance in phase formation and its interaction with the caloric effect in this specific alloy remains to be experimentally validated.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of baseline (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy and another with a 2 at% Nb addition. Process both sets identically and subject them to the same applied magnetic and pressure fields, temperature cycles and compressive loading conditions. Measure both the mechanical properties (compressive strength, fracture toughness) and the caloric response of each sample.
measurements: Compressive strength (expecting >200 MPa in Nb-modified sample)
Caloric response magnitude (should remain within ±5% of baseline)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if the Nb-modified alloy does not show a statistically significant improvement in mechanical integrity (i.e., compressive strength and fracture toughness comparable to or better than epoxy-containing composites) OR if the caloric response deviates by more than ±5% from that of the unmodified alloy under identical test conditions.

frame.system: The (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy, which in its baseline state shows excellent caloric performance under applied-field and pressure-field conditions but suffers from poor mechanical integrity and crack propagation.
frame.goal: Achieve the simultaneous combination of high caloric response and robust mechanical integrity (e.g., increased compressive strength and fracture toughness) while remaining rare‐earth–free.
frame.limitation: In the unchanged material the caloric effects are excellent, but the alloy is brittle and prone to cracking. Previous routes (epoxy-containing Mn0.98CoGe or low-melting In composites) improved either strength or heat‐transport metrics individually but did not resolve both without compromising one of the targeted properties.
root_cause_cues: gains in selected strength or heat-transport metrics
desired coexistence of robust integrity and high caloric performance remains unresolved
constraints: Single intervention (no multi-component or multi-step solutions)
the resulting system must be rare‐earth–free
the caloric response should not be sacrificed (i.e., preserved within a small quantitative variation)
the intervention should be applicable under the same applied-field, pressure-field, temperature, and loading conditions as previously reported
frame.regime: Operation under applied-fields and pressure-fields with testing performed in regimes similar to earlier compressive strength and thermal conductivity measurements (i.e., typical temperature ranges for caloric transition, and dynamic/compressive loading regimes used in prior studies)
prior_attempts: Epoxy-containing Mn0.98CoGe composites yielding compressive strengths of 152 and 218 MPa but using a polymeric binder approach that may compromise other properties
Low-melting In composites that improved thermal conductivity (over eight times that of the epoxy route) but only achieved 48 MPa compressive strength and likely altered the composite’s phase behavior
frame.understanding: It is hypothesized that the poor integrity is due to the intrinsic brittleness and an unfavorable grain-boundary/phase morphology that leads to crack initiation and propagation. By introducing a suitable microalloying element that forms a coherent, ductile secondary phase (e.g., a Nb-rich precipitate) at the grain boundaries, one could engineer a microstructure that is tougher (higher compressive strength and crack resistance) yet does not interfere with the caloric phase transformation. Supporting evidence exists from analogous systems where minor additions of ductilizing elements improved mechanical properties through in situ precipitation or grain-boundary strengthening without deleterious effects on the functional response.
frame.hypothesis: A single intervention of microalloying the (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy with approximately 2 at% Nb (or a similar rare-earth–free ductilizer) will promote the formation of a fine, ductile Nb-rich precipitate network at the grain boundaries. This network is expected to arrest crack propagation and enhance the compressive strength (targeting values >200 MPa, comparable or superior to epoxy-containing composites) while maintaining the caloric response within ±5% of that of the unmodified alloy.
frame.controlled_experiment: Prepare two batches of the alloy: one as the baseline and one with the 2 at% Nb addition. Under identical applied-field, pressure-field, temperature, and loading conditions, measure the compressive strength, fracture toughness, and caloric response. The hypothesis would be falsified if (a) the Nb-modified alloy does not show a statistically significant improvement in mechanical integrity (i.e., no improvement in compressive strength or fracture resistance compared to the baseline/epoxy composites) or (b) if the caloric effect is degraded by more than ±5% relative to the baseline.

decision.trend: Earlier studies in related high‐entropy systems have attempted to boost mechanical integrity by adding secondary phases or composite constituents. For example, TiC particles in CoCrNi alloys (PMC8402061) and nanolayered graphene interfaces in CoCrFeNi alloys (PMC9116700) have been used to arrest crack propagation and improve strength. In the MM′X family, however, interventions involving epoxy or low-melting In composites improved either compressive strength or thermal transport, but failed to simultaneously preserve the excellent caloric response. The overall trend has been to incorporate an extrinsic phase to reinforce the brittle matrix rather than modifying the alloy’s intrinsic chemistry.
decision.unsolved: A method that robustly integrates a ductile, crack‐arresting secondary phase into the (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy—thereby increasing mechanical integrity (compressive strength and toughness) without compromising the intrinsic caloric performance—remains unresolved.
decision.lever: Optimization of trace, rare‐earth–free Nb microalloying (around 2 at%) to promote in situ formation of a ductile Nb‐rich intergranular phase
decision.why: Building on the trend that extrinsic composite routes (epoxy or In additions) only partially address the performance gap, a data‐driven approach can be used to finely tune a single composition intervention. Predictive machine learning models have previously successfully mapped dopant effects on phase stability and mechanical toughness in similar alloys. By applying such a model to the (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 system under identical applied-field, pressure-field, temperature, and loading conditions, one can optimize the Nb content so that a coherent, ductile precipitate network forms at grain boundaries, enhancing compressive strength (>200 MPa) and fracture resistance while preserving the caloric response within ±5% of the baseline. A controlled experiment comparing baseline and Nb-modified samples under identical test regimes would decisively falsify or confirm this hypothesis.
